paragraphs: The last charge against the House of Representatives that I must examine rests on a supposition: that the number of members will not be increased from time to time as the growth of population may require.

It has been admitted that this objection would carry great weight if it were well supported. The following observations will show that, like most other objections to the Constitution, it can only come from an incomplete view of the subject, or from a jealousy that discolors and distorts everything it looks at.

1. Those who press the objection seem to have forgotten that the federal Constitution compares well with the State constitutions in the security it provides for a gradual increase in the number of representatives. The number that is to apply at first is declared temporary, and it lasts only three years.

A census of the inhabitants is to be repeated within every successive term of ten years. These regulations plainly have two objects. First, they readjust the apportionment of representatives to the number of inhabitants from time to time, with the single exception that each State shall have at least one representative. Second, they increase the number of representatives at the same intervals, with the sole limit that the whole number shall not exceed one for every thirty thousand inhabitants. If we review the constitutions of the individual States, we shall find that some contain no definite rules on this subject, that others correspond pretty much to the federal Constitution on this point, and that the most effective security in any of them comes down to a mere directory provision.

2. As far as experience goes on this subject, the gradual increase of representatives under the State constitutions has at least kept pace with the increase of constituents. It appears that the representatives have been as ready to agree to such measures as the constituents have been to demand them.

3. The federal Constitution has a peculiarity that ensures watchful attention, among a majority of both the people and their representatives, to a constitutional increase in the number of the latter. The peculiarity is that one branch of the legislature represents citizens and the other represents the States. In the former the larger States will therefore carry the most weight; in the latter the advantage will lie with the smaller States. From this we may infer with certainty that the larger States will strongly press for increasing the number and weight of the part of the legislature where their influence predominates. And it so happens that four of the largest States alone will hold a majority of all the votes in the House of Representatives. Suppose the representatives or people of the smaller States should at some point oppose a reasonable addition of members. A coalition of a very few States would be enough to overrule them. On ordinary occasions, rivalry and local prejudices might prevent such a coalition. But it would not fail to form when it was driven not merely by common interest but also justified by equity and the principles of the Constitution.

Perhaps it will be said that the Senate would be moved by similar motives to form an opposing coalition, and that since its agreement would be indispensable, the just and constitutional views of the other branch might be defeated. This is the difficulty that has probably caused the most serious apprehension among the jealous friends of a numerous representation. Fortunately it is one of those difficulties that exist only in appearance and vanish under close and accurate inspection. If I am not mistaken, the following reflections will be accepted as conclusive and satisfactory on this point.

The two houses will have equal authority on all legislative subjects except the origination of money bills. Even so, it cannot be doubted that the House has no small advantage in any question that turns on the relative firmness of the two houses. It has the larger number of members, it will be backed by the more powerful States, and it will speak the known and settled view of a majority of the people.

This advantage must be increased by the consciousness on one side of being supported in its demands by right, by reason and by the Constitution, and the consciousness on the other side of contending against the force of all these solemn considerations.

There is a further point. Between the smallest and the largest States there is a gradation, and several States in the middle will most likely, in general, line up with the smaller ones. Yet they are too little removed in size and population from the larger ones to back an opposition to the larger States' just and legitimate claims. Hence it is by no means certain that even in the Senate a majority of votes would be unfriendly to proper increases in the number of representatives.

It is not looking too far ahead to add that the senators from all the new States may be won over to the just views of the House of Representatives by an expedient too obvious to be overlooked. These States will grow in population with peculiar rapidity for a very long time, so they will have an interest in frequent reapportionments of representatives to the number of inhabitants. The large States, which will prevail in the House of Representatives, therefore need only make reapportionments and increases conditions of each other. The senators from all the fastest-growing States will then be bound to fight for the increases by the interest their States will feel in the reapportionments.

These considerations seem to give ample security on this subject, and ought alone to settle all the doubts and fears that have been indulged about it. Suppose, however, that they should all prove insufficient to overcome the unjust policy of the smaller States, or their predominant influence in the councils of the Senate. The larger States would still have a constitutional and infallible resource by which they could accomplish their just purposes at any time. The House of Representatives can not only refuse the supplies needed to support the government; it alone can propose them. In a word, they hold the purse. In the history of the British Constitution we see what a powerful instrument this is. By means of it an infant and humble representation of the people gradually enlarged the sphere of its activity and importance, and finally reduced, as far as it seems to have wished, all the overgrown prerogatives of the other branches of government. This power over the purse may in fact be regarded as the most complete and effective weapon that any constitution can put into the hands of the immediate representatives of the people, for obtaining redress of every grievance and carrying out every just and beneficial measure.

But will not the House of Representatives be as much interested as the Senate in keeping the government working as it should? Will it not therefore be unwilling to risk the government's existence or reputation on the Senate's giving way? Or, if such a test of firmness between the two branches were risked, would one not be as likely as the other to yield first? These questions will give no trouble to those who reflect that in every case, the smaller the number of men in power and the more lasting and conspicuous their position, the stronger the interest each of them will feel individually in whatever concerns the government. Those who represent the dignity of their country in the eyes of other nations will be especially aware of every prospect of public danger or of dishonorable stagnation in public affairs. We must ascribe to these causes the continual triumph of the British House of Commons over the other branches of the government whenever it has used the engine of a money bill. Absolute inflexibility on the part of those other branches would have thrown every department of the state into general confusion. It has neither been feared nor experienced. The greatest firmness the federal Senate or President can show will be no more than equal to a resistance in which they will be backed by constitutional and patriotic principles.

In this review of the make-up of the House of Representatives, I have passed over considerations of economy. In the present state of affairs these might have helped reduce the temporary number of representatives, and ignoring them would probably have been as rich a theme for denouncing the Constitution as the smallness of the proposed number has been. I also say nothing about the difficulty that might arise, under present circumstances, in engaging a large number of the kind of characters the people will probably elect to serve in the federal government. One observation, however, I must be allowed to add on this subject, because in my judgment it claims very serious attention. In all legislative assemblies, the greater the number of members, the fewer the men who in fact direct their proceedings. In the first place, the more numerous an assembly is, whatever characters compose it, the greater is the ascendancy of passion over reason, as is well known. In the next place, the larger the number, the greater the proportion of members with limited information and weak capacities. Now it is precisely on characters of this kind that the eloquence and skill of the few are known to work with all their force. In the ancient republics, where the whole body of the people assembled in person, a single orator or an artful statesman was generally seen to rule as completely as if a scepter had been placed in his hand alone. By the same principle, the more numerous a representative assembly is made, the more it shares the weaknesses of collective meetings of the people. Ignorance will be the dupe of cunning, and passion the slave of sophistry and declamation. The people can never make a greater mistake than to suppose that by multiplying their representatives beyond a certain limit they strengthen the barrier against government by a few. Experience will forever warn them of the opposite: AFTER SECURING A SUFFICIENT NUMBER FOR THE PURPOSES OF SAFETY, OF LOCAL INFORMATION, AND OF DIFFUSIVE SYMPATHY WITH THE WHOLE SOCIETY, they will defeat their own aims with every addition to their representatives. The face of the government may become more democratic, but the soul that animates it will be more oligarchic. The machine will be bigger, but the springs that move it will be fewer, and often more hidden.

Related to the objection about the number of representatives, and properly noted here, is another objection, about the number needed to conduct legislative business. It has been said that a quorum should have required more than a majority, and that in particular cases, if not in all, a decision should have required more than a majority of a quorum. It cannot be denied that such a precaution might have brought some advantages. It might have been an additional shield for some particular interests, and a further general obstacle to hasty and biased measures. But the drawbacks on the other side outweigh these considerations. Whenever justice or the general good might require new laws or active measures, the fundamental principle of free government would be reversed. The majority would no longer rule; power would pass to the minority. Suppose this protective privilege were limited to particular cases. A self-interested minority might use it to shield themselves from fair sacrifices for the general welfare, or, in particular emergencies, to extort unreasonable concessions. Lastly, it would make easy and encourage the harmful practice of secession. This practice has appeared even in States where only a majority is required. It undermines every principle of order and regular government, and it leads more directly to public convulsions and the ruin of popular governments than any other practice yet seen among us.
